explanation: Split the input into monotone runs and reverse each decreasing run. Merge the resulting sorted runs with a min-heap containing the next unused value from each run.
timeComplexity: O(n log(r + 1)) time for r monotone runs. Run-based languages scan n values to form runs and make n heap removals among r heads.
spaceComplexity: O(n + r) auxiliary space, including copied runs; O(n) output space. Copied runs store n entries; the merge heap stores r heads, in addition to the output.
attribution: Original Java implementation and explanation for EPI Practice, based on the displayed public contract and our independently authored C# solution; no upstream reference code adapted.
correctness: Each detected monotone run contains its original entries exactly once. Reversing a decreasing run makes it sorted without changing that multiset. During merging, the heap contains the least unused value of every nonempty run; the least remaining value overall must be one of those heads. Removing that minimum and advancing only its run preserves the invariant until every entry has been emitted.
walkthrough: The input [2, 8, 13, 10, 7, 4, 9, 15, 12] splits into [2, 8, 13], [10, 7, 4], [9, 15], [12]. Reverse the decreasing run to [4, 7, 10]. Merge the run heads: first 2, then 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 15. The result is [2, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 15].
edgeCases: An entirely increasing or decreasing array forms one sorted run after normalization.
Equal adjacent values can remain in either monotone direction without losing duplicates.
Empty and singleton arrays require no heap merging.
